clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1994
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Gordon's stroke in June 1991, within the following years: your wrist injury stopped your playing that autumn and your anxiety climbed; you and Rafe had a blow-up and he moved out; you were on your own, getting high, absorbed in radios; you felt lost and low with your grandfather gone and your mother about to remarry, unable to get going. Your functioning fell through those months. By early 1994 an exchange in Lisbon and then Porto snapped you out of it and you tore through the rest of your degree. Your cousin Bella's melanoma treatment is noted in the same months but sits outside the period since no one else's shifts gather around it.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's bowel cancer diagnosis, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Winifred being found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, within the following years: your anxiety rose and your functioning fell as you ran out of steam for performing, less content by the month; a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town left you done with performing and casting about for what came next. You were on poor terms with your family and friends, then left Thornbury for Gull Harbour and moved to Fenwick to live with Marisol; when you split up within the year you sank into a deep depression. You could not face your family and their world seemed a distance away. Your functioning stayed down through those months. Your relationship with Marisol shifted as you moved in together and then separated; you relied on friends—Corbin, Dale, Hamish, Silas—who took you in while you were back in Thornbury. By January 2004 you began swimming laps, requested help from your parents with therapy costs and returned to your therapist Victor Halloran; your functioning came back. Your grandmother died of the cancer in February 2004. Her final months in your mother's home are held outside the period since no shifts in the family gather around that note.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008–2010
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Lorna's death in January 2008, within the following months: you moved to Alder Creek for four weeks building with Silas before nursing school; you were too drained for conversation with your mother and could barely manage a phone call. She pressed to visit you, driving out regardless when you said the timing was wrong; you kept the door shut on her and the visit went wrong. Once you left for nursing school in Marlow Sound that August you stopped speaking to your mother—a cutoff that held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke in early 2009 with months of rehabilitation ahead. By August 2010 your partner's brother Leo's first child was born. The recount leaves two shifts that count: your distance from your mother in July and the cutoff when you moved in September.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, within the following years: you saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in October 2017. Your job steadied and paid well by June 2019, but by October your anxiety was up again—you constantly feel you ought to be driving your projects forward, a state you liken to all-nighters at the conservatory. You started a sleeping pill though sleep itself is no better. You aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother, a lesson from the summer at the lodge years before. By late October Wren was swamped, one thing after another—a street party, then a fundraising dinner, then the drive to the lake for her mother's retirement party. Her anxiety climbed and her functioning fell. You overfunctioned, too strict laying out a plan to settle her. Wren talks with her father and brother all day; nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. Once the weekend had a plan, she settled and the dinner went well. At the lake house that final night you were awake from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose; your symptom was up, your anxiety up, and you pulled away from her and the family. She was anxious when he'd had no sleep at family occasions. The shifts pile up in the months around the wedding and climb through the year; the gathering at the lake in late October sits within those same months and deepens the period rather than opening a new one.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
